speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Allow me to first declare that I am an equities analyst working in a financial institution in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: On that note, Mr Speaker, I rise today to speak on an issue that is very close to my heart: the future of Singapore's equities market and by extension, Singapore's role as a global financial centre.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Through this Adjournment Motion, I hope we can make Singapore equities great again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: For more than a decade, I worked as a sell-side equities analyst and observed the continual decline in the vibrancy of our capital markets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We witnessed the S-chip crisis, market shrinkage as de-listings far outstripped new initial public offerings (IPOs) and the painful erosion of investor confidence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Our market liquidity had fallen behind not just global bourses, but even regional neighbours'.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Every day, this trend affected real lives and livelihoods across our capital markets ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In 2024, I put forward the Parliamentary Question on this issue, and the Government's reply, though well-intentioned, felt insufficient.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: It lacked the bonus needed to reverse decades of decline, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong sharing that conditions remained challenging for the Singapore equities market as they are for stock exchanges in other countries.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I welcome the Government's markedly stronger resolve and put on record my appreciation to the Equities Market Review Group for its work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And I hope that this will not be a one-off measure but represents the start of a continued commitment to the Singapore market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: That said, as I shared in my Committee of Supply speech in February 2025, our measures must be bold enough to bring our equities markets into the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: However, I believe that the current recommendations by the review group may be necessary but not sufficient to truly drive permanent change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The two work-streams appear to be focused on reducing market friction rather than instituting structural interventions that improve company fundamentals in the long term.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Without three critical additional pillars, we risk repeating a familiar pattern, with Thailand’s Vayupak programme providing a cautionary tale.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Too many of our companies are delivering uncompetitive returns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: On liquidity, the difference is even more stark.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Japan has 305, Korea has 172, Hong Kong has 160.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Based on research from early 2025, 69% of Singapore-listed companies have shrunk in market capitalisation over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Only 11% of our companies have doubled their market capitalisation in 10 years, compared to 50% in Japan.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: It appears the odds are not quite in your favour when looking at investment outcomes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The review group's report states that companies that invest in building strategic shareholder value and communicate their plans effectively will attract strong investor interests.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The report contains no mandatory disclosure requirements compelling companies to demonstrate improved shareholder returns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: An EQDP fund manager told The Edge Singapore in December 2025: "At the end of the day, what we are looking for is earnings growth, ROIC   going up, ROE   going up.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: That is really what our main focus is".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Yet, our framework offers no mechanism to compel disclose commitments towards these fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As I have shared in my Committee of Supply speech in February 2025, Japan and Korea have already shown the way.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: They implemented market-wide directives, creating existential pressures on companies to perform.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In the case of Japan, in March 2023, the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) issued a formal request to companies to act on what they called management conscious of cost of capital and stock price.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This was not a good-to-have, but a structured disclosure framework with specific requirements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The TSE published a monthly list of companies by their disclosure status, creating constructive market pressure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And within a year, more than half of prime companies have disclosed initiatives, and that is now above 90%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Companies that put genuine effort into high-quality disclosures outperformed their peers by meaningful margins over the subsequent 12 months.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Korea's Value-up Program, launched in February 2024, requires companies to assess capital efficiency, set quantify ROE and ROIC targets, and disclose dividend and treasury shares plans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Korea has also amended its Commercial Act to expand directors' fiduciary duties to all shareholders and directors themselves have to be accountable now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Turning to Singapore, while the Value Unlock Programme aims to promote value creation and shareholder engagement, the key measure to achieve this is a $30 million grant.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Perhaps, small and newly listed companies may be able to benefit, but for the vast majority of companies, they can very much maintain the status quo after the review group's recommendations are implemented.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Companies face no additional disclosure or regulatory requirements to demonstrate how exactly they are going to drive higher shareholder returns or unlock value.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: At the most basic level, all listed companies should conduct formal board level assessments of capital costs, profitability and market valuation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) believes this to be important, then, I hope a clear timeline on when this may be implemented can be announced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The review group states efforts to enhance investor recourse avenues must be complemented by robust public enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: MAS will continue to work with relevant authorities to pursue and take firm actions against wrongdoers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I understand the Government's perspective that value creation is the responsibility of boards and management, not regulators.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Regulators should not micromanage, but regulators have to maintain standards that protect investors' confidence, ensure fair and timely disclosure and enforce meaningfully against wrongdoers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: To quote remarks by Mr Lim Tuang Lee, Assistant Managing Director at the MAS at the SSGI Forum in 2025, "too many companies here limit themselves to the bare minimum disclosure requirements and in doing so, miss the opportunity to articulate strategic visions and plans." My concern is that even when minimum requirements exist, companies ignore them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: SGX rules require disclosure of directors and chief executive officers' remuneration since January 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Without consequences for non-compliance, why would companies comply?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: And it is hard to blame companies for refusing to comply on this.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: After all, the stewards of our national reserves, Temasek Holdings and GIC do not have mandatory remuneration disclosures at all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I welcome the MAS announcement in May 2025 that a committee is reviewing the Code of Corporate Governance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I hope that refreshed code can hold companies accountable for disclosure lapses to instil investor confidence in our governance regime.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: On a related note, the review group advocates for a decisive shift towards a disclosure-based regime, streamlining prospectus requirements and consolidating listing reviews under SGX RegCo to improve time to market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: While reducing regulatory fiction is pro-enterprise, it raises concerns about investor protection.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I am reminded of my own experience being a sell-side analyst covering Noble Group, back when Iceberg Research wrote an exposé on alleged accounting fraud at the commodities trader.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In 2022, after years of investigation into Noble's disclosures, MAS imposed a $12.6 million civil penalty.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Although the case was undoubtedly complicated, one cannot help but feel that the penalties handed out were noticeably disproportionate to the billions that investors lost alongside the company's downfall.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Section 199 of the Securities and Futures Act requires not merely that a material statement or information was false or misleading, but that the wrongdoer either does not care whether it was true or false or knows or ought reasonably to have known that the statement of information is false or misleading in a material way.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Allow me now to pass the time to my colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, who will take us through his thoughts on a third pillar premised on macro-financial reform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As he shared, these efforts appear to be targeted toward improving market efficiency and functioning, but somehow still fall short of the sort of structural reforms necessary to foster sustained corporate value creation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chua suggested two change pillars – enhanced shareholder value, the mandatory disclosures and strengthened corporate governance with more robust enforcement – both of which address reforms to market micro-structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In closing, I will take a step back and offer a third pillar premised on macros-financial reform: enrich the capital raising life cycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our market for publicly listed stocks currently lags those of many other countries, even those with far less developed financial sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is in spite of India's overall financial development being more than two times lower than Singapore's, and Kuala Lumpur being miles away from us as a global financial centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, more worryingly, this share has steadily eroded over the past two decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Capitalisation almost reached 300% on the eve of the Global Financial Crisis, but this has steadily eroded by more than three-fifths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This trend is heading in precisely the wrong direction if the goal is to fortify our stock market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nor should we rest easy just because of SGX's recent performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The SGX certainly did well last year, posting returns closer to 30%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But so did the stock exchanges of Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Vietnam – and few would claim that these markets are the benchmarks we should aspire to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Returns are distinct from liquidity and the primary role of any stock market is to raise capital to fund investments, with returns being secondary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even when scaled to per capita terms, we fall short of a country, like Israel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, while we are deniably successful within East Asia, we remain a distance behind the global leaders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's financial market debt is four-fifths those of South Korea, an economy whose financial developed markets are typically regarded as less sophisticated than ours, and only a little more than half that of Hong Kong, our major financial centre competitor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we have made headway in certain segments, notably foreign exchange and real estate, our financial markets still fall short in one of the key functions – to raise funds for doing business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Improving the life cycle for capital raising, therefore, requires us to look at the full stack for corporate finance – from angel through different stages of venture investments by private equities to IPOs on the secondary board followed by possible graduation to the main board.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are close to two dozen angel and seed investment networks here, of which the most prominent, the Singapore Angel Network and the Business Angel Network of Southeast Asia, are well established.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The funding environment is liquid with hundreds of deals annually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, four in five investors even report optimism about the ecosystem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has also extended significant support to the startup scene.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is both grant money as well as tax breaks for angel investments and co-investment opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Officially sanctioned hubs abound, such as Block 71 and Stage One, along with other incubators and accelerators located in the One-North complex.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The National Research Foundation has also been active in supporting innovations in deep technology, including the launch of the $50 million Graduate Innovation Research Programme to support locally based entrepreneurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given this backdrop, the stage for this stage of the venture cycle appears well positioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I, therefore, second the recent decision by Temasek to back away from directing exposures to early stage investing and instead focus on later stage, meaning Series B and later funding rounds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is logical given Temasek's relative size which makes deploying relatively small sums of capital challenging and potentially, inefficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is also vital that the institution deepened domestic liquidity for later venture capital stages, which leads me to favour an even stronger focus on the pre-IPO stage with a clearer mandate to target locally based companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will help catalyse the market for private investor exit while simultaneously easing the transition of firms to public investment on the secondary board.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are already some Government-directed efforts on this front, the $1.5 billion Anchor Fund @ 65 and $500 million Growth IPO Fund have been in place since 2022 to support high growth firms with public listings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, such efforts are relatively small and perhaps, more importantly, incomplete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather than one-offs, what is needed to generate market activity is continuous reinvestment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will be better to simply enfold these entirely into Temasek's overall portfolio while channelling the fund toward funding more domestic opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The goal is to usher companies toward an eventual listing and to choose SGX as their outlet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, the fate of our main board will ultimately be tied and dependent on how vibrant our secondary board is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The problem is one of chicken and egg.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presently, low liquidity has made venture capitalists wary of listing on this board, while the small number of new listings in turn limits trading and turnover, thereby becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MAS has also tabled proposals for streamlining primary and secondary listings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a positive step which I support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We may also consider piling on financial incentives, such as granting firms that may choose to list continued recognition as SMEs for tax purposes over an interim period as an additional inducement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I should stress that easing listing requirements does not imply weaker regulation in the long run, contrary to the points made by my hon friend about transparent disclosures and strengthen governance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, I am arguing for initial forbearance to strengthen incentives to list here in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may be further refined to require a minimum allocation to onshore allocations specifically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can also do more with other private sector institutional accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are excellent examples of stakeholder capitalism around the world, including Germany, Japan and Scandinavia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Setting aside advantages and disadvantages of such arrangements, it is difficult to deny that channelling more buy-side exposure toward the SGX would likely improve market depth and foster greater vibrancy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To encourage take-up, we could grant tax-free status for employee stock ownerships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We could even consider giving further inducements to retail investors to leverage the participation of average households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One in two Singaporeans already own stocks and half of the local exchange is already held by individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Central Provident Fund Investment Scheme already allows an opt-in for Singapore-listed shares on the SGX.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will be a small leap to further promote responsible retail ownership of the local market index, ideally through revisions in the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS) or through additional educational incentives, either associated with the LRIS or independently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sweden has demonstrated that such bottom-up participation can underpin stock market success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the supply side, we can also develop a deeper pool of front office talent necessary to ensure a robust financial ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We welcome such feedback as part of the ongoing efforts to make our equities market more competitive.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am pleased to report that we are making good progress with our review and have achieved some initial success.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The average daily traded value of securities in 2025 was the highest since 2010.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Recently, the number of Singapore-listed stocks with at least $1 million in average daily trading turnover has risen to 100.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is an increase of 40% compared to August 2024 when we formed the review group.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The total market value of listed companies on SGX also crossed the $1 trillion mark.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Despite global uncertainties, the Straits Times Index (STI) delivered strong returns last year, with over 28% total returns.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And over five years, STI's total returns exceeded 100% in Singapore-dollars terms, outperforming many regional markets.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As global investors rebalance and diversify across Asia, Singapore's reputation as a safe, trusted financial centre, with a strong and stable Singapore dollar, has drawn growing interest.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we know markets have ups and downs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our focus, therefore, must be to continue strengthening the competitiveness and attractiveness of our ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have worked closely with the industry to co-create solutions and implement a holistic package that strengthens both demand and supply, as well as enhancing greater connectivity that supports efficient trading.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the past 18 months, the Equities Market Review Group engaged widely with brokers, banks, asset managers, listed companies, prospective issuers, research providers and industry bodies and this process helped us to move beyond making individual tweaks towards a comprehensive set of mutually reinforcing moves, to get the momentum of the flywheel going.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will focus on effective and timely implementation to translate policy ideas into market outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To support this important area of work, we have established an Equity Market Implementation Committee, co-chaired by MAS and SGX.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of the measures have already been rolled out.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other initiatives are on track and will be implemented over the course of the year as we modernise market infrastructure and launch new market connectivity initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, innovation in policy requires taking calculated risks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We adopted an approach of allowing for more risk-taking in the equities market review, and with support from Singaporeans and Members of this House, the Government will do likewise for other areas too.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As we push boundaries and take bold steps to try new ideas, we will put in place guardrails, where necessary, to protect against downside risks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will devote more resources into public and investor education, working with partners, like the SGX Academy and the Securities Investors Association (Singapore), so that stakeholders understand that while taking more risks could yield higher investment returns, they are also prepared to face greater market volatility.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This trade-off is relevant when we decide on our personal and family investments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is also applicable when we decide on the level of risks we want to collectively take as a country.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When we shift towards a more disclosure-based regime, with regulation that is more focused and facilitative, we will continue to seek high quality listings and provide adequate and timely information for investors to make their decisions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Key stakeholders in the ecosystem must also exercise their respective areas of expertise and responsibility – IPO professionals and research analysts have to uphold high standards of due diligence and analysis to support investors in making informed decisions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MAS will take steps to strengthen investor confidence, such as encouraging transparency and shareholder engagements through initiatives under the Value Unlock Programme, while enhancing investor protection mechanisms, especially for retail investors, such as strengthening their options for recourse against misconduct.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I take Mr Louis Chua's point that some requirements may have to be mandatory, and we are certainly open to looking at these examples.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I hope Mr Chua will agree with me that not everything that can add value to the company needs to be mandated because the companies themselves would have strong commercial interest to want to make sure they can increase their market value.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To maintain trust and confidence in our markets, MAS and the relevant authorities in Singapore will continue to work closely on robust investigation, market surveillance and timely enforcement against breaches of disclosure requirements and market misconduct.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also made decisive moves to enhance international connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The SGX-Nasdaq Global Listing Board, when implemented later this year, will enable eligible companies to simultaneously list on both exchanges with one set of prospectus.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This can help support their growth plans, widen their investor base and enhance liquidity across time zones.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is like a never-ending marathon that you just have to keep running.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to listen, adapt and raise our game in partnership with the industry.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I certainly also welcome feedback and suggestions from Mr Chua, from Assoc Prof Lim and their colleagues from the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Although our efforts have yielded some initial success, we cannot stand still and rest on our laurels because the competition for global capital is intense and fast evolving.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must continue to play to our strengths and we must continue to innovate to stay ahead, or we will risk falling behind and being over-taken.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In English): Learning is like rowing upstream; to not advance is to fall behind.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are not trying to go for a silver bullet that can, on its own, solve all the problems.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Assoc Prof Lim is right that we also need to look at how the market can facilitate companies to grow.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I hope Assoc Prof Lim will agree with me that if you do not have good shareholder returns, you would not be able to achieve that outcome.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Pursuant to Standing Order 2(3)(a), I wish to inform hon Members that the Sitting tomorrow will commence at 1.30 pm.
